Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the systems, pursuant to paragraphs 3 and 6. Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support. The obligations set out in paragraphs 1 and 2, are without prejudice to other deployer obligations under Union or national law and to the deployer’s freedom to organise its own resources and activities for the purpose of implementing the human oversight measures indicated by the provider. Without prejudice to paragraphs 1 and 2, to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data, that deployer shall ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, inform providers in accordance with Article 72. Where deployers have reason to consider that the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions may result in that AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system. Where deployers have identified a serious incident, they shall also immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities of that incident. If the deployer is not able to reach the provider, Article 73 shall applymutatis mutandis. This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers of AI systems which are law enforcement authorities. For deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation set out in the first subparagraph shall be deemed to be fulfilled by complying with the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial service law. Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data. Deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law shall maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law. Before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, deployers who are employers shall inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system. This information shall be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on information of workers and their representatives. Deployers of high-risk AI systems that are public authorities, or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies shall comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49. When such deployers find that the high-risk AI system that they envisage using has not been registered in the EU database referred to in Article 71, they shall not use that system and shall inform the provider or the distributor. Without prejudice to Directive (EU) 2016/680, in the framework of an investigation for the targeted search of a person suspected or convicted of having committed a criminal offence, the deployer of a high-risk AI system for post-remote biometric identification shall request an authorisation,ex ante, or without undue delay and no later than 48 hours, by a judicial authority or an administrative authority whose decision is binding and subject to judicial review, for the use of that system, except when it is used for the initial identification of a potential suspect based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to the offence. Each use shall be limited to what is strictly necessary for the investigation of a specific criminal offence. If the authorisation requested pursuant to the first subparagraph is rejected, the use of the post-remote biometric identification system linked to that requested authorisation shall be stopped with immediate effect and the personal data linked to the use of the high-risk AI system for which the authorisation was requested shall be deleted. In no case shall such high-risk AI system for post-remote biometric identification be used for law enforcement purposes in an untargeted way, without any link to a criminal offence, a criminal proceeding, a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a criminal offence, or the search for a specific missing person. It shall be ensured that no decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken by the law enforcement authorities based solely on the output of such post-remote biometric identification systems. This paragraph is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 for the processing of biometric data. Regardless of the purpose or deployer, each use of such high-risk AI systems shall be documented in the relevant police file and shall be made available to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority upon request, excluding the disclosure of sensitive operational data related to law enforcement. question: What technical solutions must high-risk AI systems implement to address AI-specific vulnerabilities?
expected_answer: Under Article 15(5) of the EU AI Act, high-risk AI systems must be engineered with specialized cybersecurity measures to resist attempts by unauthorized third parties to manipulate their behavior, outputs, or performance. Beyond traditional IT security, providers are required to implement technical solutions that specifically address AI-vulnerabilities through a cycle of prevention, detection, and response. These measures must target sophisticated threats such as data poisoning (manipulating training sets), model poisoning (tampering with pre-trained components), and adversarial examples (inputs designed to trick the model into making errors, also known as model evasion). Additionally, the system must be resilient against confidentiality attacks aimed at extracting sensitive model parameters or data, ensuring that the AI remains secure and reliable throughout its entire operational lifecycle.

question: What is the role of the 'European AI Office'?
expected_answer: Under the EU AI Act, the European AI Office serves as the central hub of expertise and the primary regulatory body for AI governance at the Union level. Established within the European Commission, its role is twofold: it is responsible for the supervision and enforcement of rules concerning general-purpose AI (GPAI) models—particularly those posing systemic risks—and it coordinates the consistent application of the Act across all Member States. The Office develops technical tools, benchmarks, and codes of practice to evaluate AI capabilities while supporting national authorities in their market surveillance tasks. By fostering a "European ecosystem" of trustworthy AI, the Office acts as the bridge between high-level policy and practical implementation, ensuring that AI development aligns with EU values of safety and fundamental rights.

question: What are the transparency rules for AI systems used for text generation?
expected_answer: Generation of audio, image, video or text content should be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
Advanced_Response:
The transparency rules for AI systems generating text are detailed in Article [1] of the provided context. These rules establish obligations for both the providers and the deployers of such systems.

**Obligations for Providers:**

*   Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic text content must ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

**Obligations for Deployers (Specific Contexts):**

*   **Public Interest Information:** Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated.
*   **Timing of Information:** The information regarding the AI system must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure.

**Exceptions and Limitations:**

The transparency obligations are subject to several exceptions:

*   **General Output Marking Exception:** The obligation to mark outputs does not apply to the extent that the AI systems:
    *   Perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data or the semantics thereof.
    *   Are authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences.
*   **Public Interest Text Disclosure Exception:** The obligation to disclose artificially generated or manipulated text published on matters of public interest does not apply where:
    *   The use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offence.
    *   The AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control, and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.

question: What specific powers must human overseers of high-risk AI have?
expected_answer: Human oversight must be provided to ensure that individuals can fully understand the system's capacities and limitations, correctly interpret the outputs, and remain able to disregard, override, or reverse those outputs.
Advanced_Response:
The context specifies that human oversight must be assigned to natural persons who possess the necessary competence, training, and authority (Article eu_ai_act_art_26). Furthermore, Article eu_ai_act_art_14 details that the high-risk AI system must be provided to the deployer in a way that natural persons assigned human oversight are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate, to perform the following actions:

*   Properly understand the relevant capacities and limitations of the high-risk AI system and monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions, and unexpected performance.
*   Remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the output produced by the high-risk AI system (automation bias).
*   Correctly interpret the high-risk AI system’s output, taking into account available interpretation tools and methods.
*   Decide, in any particular situation, to not use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override, or reverse its output.
*   Intervene in the operation of the high-risk AI system or interrupt the system through a ‘stop’ button or a similar procedure that allows the system to come to a halt in a safe state.

Additionally, for high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, the measures must ensure that no action or decision is taken based on the identification resulting from the system unless that identification has been separately verified and confirmed by at least two natural persons with the necessary competence, training, and authority (Article eu_ai_act_art_14).

Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure they use such systems in accordance with the instructions for use accompanying the systems, pursuant to paragraphs 3 and 6. Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support. The obligations set out in paragraphs 1 and 2, are without prejudice to other deployer obligations under Union or national law and to the deployer’s freedom to organise its own resources and activities for the purpose of implementing the human oversight measures indicated by the provider. Without prejudice to paragraphs 1 and 2, to the extent the deployer exercises control over the input data, that deployer shall ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Deployers shall monitor the operation of the high-risk AI system on the basis of the instructions for use and, where relevant, inform providers in accordance with Article 72. Where deployers have reason to consider that the use of the high-risk AI system in accordance with the instructions may result in that AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1), they shall, without undue delay, inform the provider or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authority, and shall suspend the use of that system. Where deployers have identified a serious incident, they shall also immediately inform first the provider, and then the importer or distributor and the relevant market surveillance authorities of that incident. If the deployer is not able to reach the provider, Article 73 shall applymutatis mutandis. This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers of AI systems which are law enforcement authorities. For deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law, the monitoring obligation set out in the first subparagraph shall be deemed to be fulfilled by complying with the rules on internal governance arrangements, processes and mechanisms pursuant to the relevant financial service law. Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data. Deployers that are financial institutions subject to requirements regarding their internal governance, arrangements or processes under Union financial services law shall maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law. Before putting into service or using a high-risk AI system at the workplace, deployers who are employers shall inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to the use of the high-risk AI system. This information shall be provided, where applicable, in accordance with the rules and procedures laid down in Union and national law and practice on information of workers and their representatives. Deployers of high-risk AI systems that are public authorities, or Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies shall comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49. When such deployers find that the high-risk AI system that they envisage using has not been registered in the EU database referred to in Article 71, they shall not use that system and shall inform the provider or the distributor. It shall be ensured that no decision that produces an adverse legal effect on a person may be taken by the law enforcement authorities based solely on the output of such post-remote biometric identification systems. This paragraph is without prejudice to Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 and Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 for the processing of biometric data. The role of 'Trusted Flaggers' under the Digital Services Act (DSA) involves submitting notices regarding allegedly illegal content and adhering to specific operational and reporting obligations.

**Criteria for Obtaining Status:**
The status of 'trusted flagger' is awarded by the Digital Services Coordinator of the Member State where the applicant is established, provided the applicant demonstrates meeting all of the following conditions:
*   Possessing particular expertise and competence for detecting, identifying, and notifying illegal content.
*   Maintaining independence from any provider of online platforms.
*   Carrying out activities for the purpose of submitting notices diligently, accurately, and objectively.

*   **Notice Submission:** Trusted flaggers submit notices through the mechanisms referred to in Article 16.

    *   The identity of the provider of hosting services.
    *   The type of allegedly illegal content notified.
    *   The action taken by the provider.
*   **Report Submission and Availability:** These reports must be sent to the awarding Digital Services Coordinator and made publicly available. The information contained within these reports must not include personal data.

Providers of online platforms are obligated to take necessary technical and organizational measures to ensure that notices submitted by trusted flaggers, acting within their designated area of expertise, through the Article 16 mechanisms, are:
*   Given priority.
*   Processed and decided upon without undue delay (Article eu_dsa_act_art_22_par_1).

question: What is the primary requirement for the risk management system of high-risk AI?
expected_answer: High-risk AI systems require continuous review throughout the AI's lifecycle and should identify and analyze potential risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights, estimate and evaluate these risks, and adopt measures to manage them. It should ensure that remaining risks are acceptable and minimized as much as possible.
Advanced_Response:
The primary requirement for the risk management system of high-risk AI systems is that it must be established, implemented, documented, and maintained throughout the entire lifecycle of the system, functioning as a continuous iterative process that requires regular systematic review and updating (Article eu_ai_act_art_9).

This system shall comprise the following steps:

*   Identification and analysis of the known and reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system may pose to health, safety, or fundamental rights when used according to its intended purpose.
*   Elimination or reduction of identified risks, where technically feasible, through adequate design and development of the high-risk AI system.
*   Estimation and evaluation of risks that may emerge when the system is used as intended, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse.
*   Implementation of adequate mitigation and control measures for risks that cannot be eliminated.
*   Evaluation of other possible risks, based on data gathered from the post-market monitoring system referred to in Article 72.
*   Provision of information required pursuant to Article 13, and, where appropriate, training for deployers.
*   Adoption of appropriate and targeted risk management measures designed to address the identified risks.

Furthermore, the risk management measures must ensure that:

*   Due consideration is given to the technical knowledge, experience, education, the expected training by the deployer, and the presumed context of use when eliminating or reducing risks.
*   The relevant residual risk associated with each hazard, and the overall residual risk of the high-risk AI system, is judged to be acceptable.

question: What is the transparency requirement for AI systems interacting with natural persons?
expected_answer: Companies must inform users when they are interacting with an AI system, unless it's obvious or the AI is used for legal purposes like crime detection. AI systems that create synthetic content (like deepfakes) must mark their outputs as artificially generated.
Advanced_Response:
The transparency requirements for AI systems interacting with natural persons are detailed across several provisions, depending on the nature of the interaction or the content generated.

**General Interaction Transparency:**

*   Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system.
*   This obligation is waived if the interaction is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant, and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use (Article eu_ai_act_art_50 and Paragraph eu_ai_act_art_50_par_1).

**Transparency for Generated or Manipulated Content:**

*   **Synthetic Content:** Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article eu_ai_act_art_50).
*   **Deep Fakes/Manipulation:** Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a *deep fake* must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offence (Article eu_ai_act_art_50).
*   **Public Interest Text:** Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated, unless the use is authorized by law for criminal investigation or if the content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control, and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication (Article eu_ai_act_art_50).

**Timing and Format of Disclosure:**

*   The information regarding these transparency obligations must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and it must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article eu_ai_act_art_50).

**Specific Obligations for Certain Systems:**

*   **Emotion Recognition/Biometric Categorisation:** Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorisation system must inform the natural persons exposed to the operation of the system (Article eu_ai_act_art_50).
*   **High-Risk Systems (General):** For high-risk AI systems, deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons who possess the necessary competence, training, and authority (Article eu_ai_act_art_26).

The transparency requirements for AI systems interacting with natural persons are detailed in Article eu_ai_act_art_50.

The obligations include:

**1. General Interaction Transparency:**
*   Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system.
*   This obligation is waived if the interaction is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant, and circumspect, considering the context of use (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraph 1).

**2. Transparency for Generated or Manipulated Content:**
Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must ensure that the outputs are:
*   Marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraph 2).

**3. Specific System Disclosure Obligations:**
*   **Deep Fakes:** Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraph 2).
*   **Public Interest Text:** Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest must disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraph 2).
*   **Emotion Recognition/Biometric Categorization:** Deployers of an emotion recognition system or a biometric categorization system must inform the natural persons exposed to the system about its operation (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraph 2).

**4. Manner and Timing of Information:**
*   The information referred to in Article eu_ai_act_art_50 must be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure, and must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraph 2).

**Exemptions:**
The transparency obligations are subject to several exceptions, including:
*   When the use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offence (subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties) (Article eu_ai_act_art_50, paragraphs 1 and 2).

Advanced_Response:
The transparency reporting obligations for online platforms are detailed under the Digital Services Act (DSA) and vary depending on the specific type of provider (e.g., general intermediary service, online platform, or very large online platform).

### General Reporting Obligations (Intermediary Services)

Providers of intermediary services must make publicly available, at least once a year, clear, easily comprehensible reports on content moderation engaged in during the relevant period, which must include, as applicable:

*   **Orders from Authorities:** The number of orders received from Member States’ authorities (including those issued under Articles 9 and 10), categorized by the type of illegal content, the issuing Member State, and the median time needed to inform the authority or give effect to the order.
*   **Hosting Services Notices:** For hosting services, the number of notices submitted under Article 16, categorized by the type of alleged illegal content, the number from trusted flaggers, the action taken (differentiating if the action was based on law or terms and conditions), the number of notices processed using automated means, and the median time needed for action.
*   **Own Initiative Moderation:** Meaningful and comprehensible information about moderation conducted at the provider’s own initiative, including:
    *   The use of automated tools.
    *   Measures taken to provide training and assistance to content moderation staff.
    *   The number and type of measures affecting the availability, visibility, and accessibility of information.
*   **General Categorization:** The reported information must be categorized by the type of illegal content or violation of the service provider’s terms and conditions, by the detection method, and by the type of restriction applied.
*   **Complaints Handling:** The number of complaints received through internal complaint-handling systems, along with the basis for complaints, decisions taken, the median time needed for those decisions, and the number of instances where decisions were reversed.
*   **Automated Means Use:** Any use of automated means for content moderation must include a qualitative description, the precise purposes, indicators of the accuracy, the possible rate of error, and any safeguards applied.

*(Note: These obligations do not apply to micro or small enterprises that are not very large online platforms.)*

### Obligations for Online Platforms (General)

Providers of online platforms must also include in their reports:

*   The number of disputes submitted to out-of-court dispute settlement bodies, the outcomes of the dispute settlement, the median time needed for completing the dispute settlement procedures, and the share of disputes where the provider implemented the decisions.
*   The number of suspensions imposed, distinguishing between suspensions enacted for:
    *   The provision of manifestly illegal content.
    *   The submission of manifestly unfounded notices.
    *   The submission of manifestly unfounded complaints.
*   **Recipient Data:** By 17 February 2023, and at least every six months thereafter, they must publish information on the average monthly active recipients of the service in the Union.
*   **Database Submission:** Providers of online platforms must submit decisions and statements of reasons referred to in Article 17(1) to a publicly accessible machine-readable database managed by the Commission.

### Enhanced Obligations for Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs)

Providers of very large online platforms or very large online search engines have additional reporting requirements:

*   **Reporting Frequency:** They must publish reports (referred to in Article 15) at least every six months.
*   **Specific Content:** These reports must additionally specify:
    *   The human resources dedicated to content moderation in the Union, broken down by each official language, including compliance with Articles 16, 22, and 20.
    *   The qualifications and linguistic expertise of the staff performing content moderation, along with the training and support provided.
    *   Indicators of accuracy (from Article 15(1), point (e)), broken down by each official language.
    *   The average monthly recipients of the service for each Member State.
*   **Regulatory Submissions:** They must transmit to the Digital Services Coordinator of establishment and the Commission, and make publicly available, reports detailing:
    *   The results of the risk assessment pursuant to Article 34.
    *   The specific mitigation measures put in place pursuant to Article 35(1).
    *   The audit report provided for in Article 37(4).
    *   The audit implementation report provided for in Article 37(6).

The transparency reporting obligations for online platforms vary depending on whether the platform is a general provider or a Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) or search engine.

**For Providers of Online Platforms (General Obligations):**

Providers of online platforms must adhere to the following reporting requirements, as detailed in Article eu_dsa_act_art_24:

*   **General Reporting:** They must publish information regarding their activities (Article eu_dsa_act_art_24_par_1).
*   **Dispute Settlement Information:** In addition to the information required under Article 15, the reports must include:
    *   The number of disputes submitted to the out-of-court dispute settlement bodies referred to in Article eu_dsa_act_art_39.
    *   The outcomes of the dispute settlement.
    *   The median time needed for completing the dispute settlement procedures.
    *   The share of disputes where the provider implemented the decisions of the body.
    *   The number of suspensions imposed pursuant to Article eu_dsa_act_art_23, distinguishing between suspensions for:
        *   Manifestly illegal content.
        *   Submission of manifestly unfounded notices.
        *   Submission of manifestly unfounded complaints.
*   **Average Monthly Active Recipients:** By 17 February 2023 and at least once every six months thereafter, providers must publish information on the average monthly active recipients of the service in the Union. This calculation must be an average over the past six months and follow the methodology laid down in the delegated acts referred to in Article eu_dsa_act_art_33(3) (Article eu_dsa_act_art_24_par_2).
*   **Submission to Commission:** Providers must submit the decisions and statements of reasons referred to in Article eu_dsa_act_art_17 to the Commission for inclusion in a publicly accessible machine-readable database (Article eu_dsa_act_art_24_par_5).

Providers of very large online platforms or search engines must publish reports (referring to Article 15 and Article 24(1)) at least every six months (Article eu_dsa_act_art_42_par_1). These reports must additionally specify:

*   **Human Resources:** The human resources dedicated to content moderation in respect of the service offered in the Union, broken down by each applicable official language (including compliance with Articles eu_dsa_act_art_16, eu_dsa_act_art_22, and eu_dsa_act_art_20).
*   **Staff Expertise:** The qualifications and linguistic expertise of the persons carrying out content moderation activities, as well as the training and support provided to such staff.
*   **Accuracy Indicators:** The indicators of accuracy and related information referred to in Article eu_dsa_act_art_15(1), point (e), broken down by each official language.
*   **Recipient Data:** Information on the average monthly recipients of the service for *each* Member State, in addition to the information required under Article eu_dsa_act_art_24(2).
*   **Risk and Audit Reporting:** They must transmit and make publicly available reports concerning:
    *   The results of the risk assessment pursuant to Article eu_dsa_act_art_34.
    *   The specific mitigation measures put in place pursuant to Article eu_dsa_act_art_35(1).
    *   The audit report provided for in Article eu_dsa_act_art_37(4) and the audit implementation report provided for in Article eu_dsa_act_art_37(6) (Article eu_dsa_act_art_42_par_3).

These measures may include, where applicable, the following:

*   **Service Adaptation:**
    *   Adapting the design, features, or functioning of their services, including their online interfaces.
    *   Adapting their terms and conditions and their enforcement.
*   **Content Moderation:**
    *   Adapting content moderation processes, including the speed and quality of processing notices related to specific types of illegal content, and the expeditious removal of, or the disabling of access to, notified content (particularly regarding illegal hate speech or cyber violence).
    *   Adapting any relevant decision-making processes and dedicated resources for content moderation.
*   **Algorithmic and Advertising Systems:**
    *   Testing and adapting their algorithmic systems, including their recommender systems.
    *   Adapting their advertising systems and adopting targeted measures aimed at limiting or adjusting the presentation of advertisements.

    *   Reinforcing internal processes, resources, testing, documentation, or supervision of any activity, particularly concerning the detection of systemic risk.

question: What is the obligation for VLOPs regarding data access for researchers?
expected_answer: Very Large Online Platforms are required to provide data access for researchers for the sole purpose of conducting research that contributes to the detection, identification and understanding of systemic risks in the EU.
Advanced_Response:
The obligations for providers of very large online platforms or of very large online search engines (VLOPs) regarding data access for researchers are primarily detailed in Article eu_dsa_act_art_40 of the Digital Services Act.

The obligations include:

*   **Provision of Data Access:** VLOPs shall provide access to data to vetted researchers upon a reasoned request from the Digital Services Coordinator of establishment.
*   **Purpose Limitation:** This access must be for the sole purpose of conducting research that contributes to:
    *   The detection, identification, and understanding of systemic risks in the Union, as set out pursuant to Article 34(1).
    *   The assessment of the adequacy, efficiency, and impacts of the risk mitigation measures pursuant to Article 35.
*   **Timeline:** The data must be provided within a reasonable period specified in the request.
*   **Mechanism of Access:** VLOPs must facilitate and provide access to the data pursuant to paragraphs 1 and 4 through appropriate interfaces specified in the request, including online databases or application programming interfaces.
*   **Immediate Access (Publicly Available Data):** VLOPs must give access without undue delay to data, including, where technically possible, to real-time data, provided that the data is publicly accessible in their online interface by researchers who comply with the conditions set out in paragraph 8, points (b), (c), (d), and (e), and who use the data solely for performing research that contributes to the detection, identification, and understanding of systemic risks in the Union pursuant to Article 34(1).

These obligations are contingent upon the researchers meeting the requirements to be granted the status of ‘vetted researchers’ as outlined in Article eu_dsa_act_art_40.

Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They shall have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. Those characteristics of the data sets may be met at the level of individual data sets or at the level of a combination thereof. question: What are the additional obligations for providers of GPAI models with systemic risk?
expected_answer: Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risks must evaluate their models using standard protocols, identify and reduce systemic risks, and report any serious incidents to the AI Office and national authorities. They must also ensure their AI models and infrastructure are secure.
Advanced_Response:
Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk have additional obligations, in addition to those listed in Articles 53 and 54, as detailed in Article 55. These obligations include:

*   **Model Evaluation:** Performing model evaluation in accordance with standardized protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, which includes conducting and documenting adversarial testing of the model to identify and mitigate systemic risks.
*   **Risk Assessment and Mitigation:** Assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at Union level, including their sources, that may arise from the development, placing on the market, or use of the general-purpose AI models.
*   **Incident Reporting:** Keeping track of, documenting, and reporting, without undue delay, to the AI Office and, where appropriate, to national competent authorities, relevant information concerning serious incidents and possible corrective measures to address them.
*   **Cybersecurity:** Ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the general-purpose AI model with systemic risk and its physical infrastructure.

Furthermore, providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk may rely on codes of practice under Article 56 or compliance with European harmonised standards to demonstrate compliance with these obligations, until a harmonised standard is published.

The role of harmonised standards in high-risk AI compliance is multifaceted, primarily establishing a presumption of conformity and forming a basis for conformity assessment procedures.

The specific roles include:

*   **Presumption of Conformity:**
    *   High-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models that are in conformity with harmonised standards (whose references are published in the Official Journal of the European Union in accordance with Regulation (EU) No 1025/2012) shall be **presumed** to be in conformity with the requirements set out in Section 2 of the Chapter, or, where applicable, with the obligations set out in Chapter V, Sections 2 and 3, to the extent that those standards cover those requirements or obligations (Article eu_ai_act_art_40).
    *   Similarly, high-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models conforming to common specifications (which are related to the standardisation process) shall be **presumed** to be in conformity with the requirements set out in Section 2 of the Chapter, or, where applicable, to comply with the obligations set out in Sections 2 and 3 of Chapter V, to the extent those common specifications cover those requirements or obligations (Article eu_ai_act_art_41).

*   **Basis for Conformity Assessment:**
    *   For high-risk AI systems, if the provider has applied harmonised standards referred to in Article 40, the provider may opt for specific conformity assessment procedures (Article eu_ai_act_art_43).
    *   In certain instances, if the provider has not applied, or has only partially applied, the harmonised standard, other procedures must be followed (Article eu_ai_act_art_43).

*   **Standardisation Process:**
    *   The Commission is responsible for issuing standardisation requests covering the requirements set out in Section 2 of the Chapter and Chapter V, Sections 2 and 3, to European standardisation organisations (Article eu_ai_act_art_40).
    *   The Commission shall request that these standards ensure that high-risk AI systems or general-purpose AI models placed on the market or put into service in the Union meet the relevant requirements or obligations laid down in the Regulation (Article eu_ai_act_art_40).

*   For the conformity assessment procedure referred to in Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body.

### Conformity Assessment Procedures (Article eu_ai_act_art_43)

The required procedure depends on the specific high-risk AI system and the compliance measures applied by the provider:

**1. For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III:**
The provider must select one of the following conformity assessment procedures:
*   The procedure set out in Annex VII.
*   The internal control referred to in Annex VI.
*   The assessment of the quality management system and the technical documentation, involving a notified body, if harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41) are not available.

**2. Selection Criteria for Annex VII:**
When following the procedure in Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, unless the system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or by Union institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, in which case the market surveillance authority (Article 74(8) or (9)) acts as the notified body. The choice of procedure under Annex VII is determined by whether the provider has:
*   Applied harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41).
*   Not applied, or only partially applied, the harmonised standard, or if common specifications exist but were not applied.
*   Applied only the restricted part of a harmonised standard published with a restriction.

**3. For high-risk AI systems (points 2 to 8 of Annex III):**
Providers must follow the conformity assessment procedure based on internal control as referred to in Annex VI, which does not require the involvement of a notified body.

**4. For systems covered by Union harmonisation legislation:**
The provider must follow the relevant conformity assessment procedure mandated by those specific legal acts.

**General Requirements:**
*   The requirements set out in Section 2 of the Chapter apply to the assessment.
*   Points 4.3., 4.4., 4.5., and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also apply.

**Key Procedural Notes:**
*   **Substantial Modification:** A new conformity assessment procedure is required for a substantial modification, irrespective of whether the modified system is intended for further distribution or continued use.
*   **Learning Systems:** Changes to the high-risk AI system and its performance that were pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment and are documented in Annex IV, point 2(f), do not constitute a substantial modification.
*   **Opt-Out Provision:** If a legal act allows a product manufacturer to opt out of a third-party conformity assessment, the manufacturer must still apply all harmonised standards or common specifications covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of the Chapter.

### Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (Article eu_ai_act_art_9)

For the first use of a high-risk AI system, deployers who are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III, must perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights. This assessment must include:
*   A description of the deployer’s processes using the system.
*   The intended period of time and frequency of use.
*   The categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected.
*   The specific risks of harm likely to impact the identified categories, considering information from the provider (Article 13).
*   A description of human oversight measures.
*   Measures to be taken if risks materialize, including internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

Advanced_Response:
The obligations related to crisis response for Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) are detailed under provisions concerning voluntary crisis protocols and mandatory actions adopted by the Commission during a crisis.

**Under Voluntary Crisis Protocols (Article eu_dsa_act_art_48):**
The Commission shall aim to ensure that voluntary crisis protocols involving VLOPs include measures such as:
*   Prominently displaying information on the crisis situation provided by Member States’ authorities or at Union level, or by other relevant reliable bodies.
*   Ensuring the provider designates a specific point of contact for crisis management; for VLOPs/VLOSs, this may be the compliance officer referred to in Article 41.
*   Adapting resources dedicated to compliance with the obligations set out in Articles 16, 20, 22, 23, and 35 to the needs arising from the crisis situation.

Furthermore, the crisis protocols set out clearly must include:
*   The specific parameters defining the extraordinary circumstance and the objectives pursued.
*   The role of each participant and the measures they are to put in place.
*   A clear procedure for determining when the protocol is to be activated and the period for which measures are to be taken.
*   Safeguards addressing any negative effects on fundamental rights, particularly the freedom of expression and information and the right to non-discrimination.
*   A process to publicly report on any measures taken, their duration, and their outcomes, upon the termination of the crisis situation.

**Under Commission-Mandated Actions During a Crisis (Article eu_dsa_act_art_36):**
Where a crisis occurs (defined as extraordinary circumstances leading to a serious threat to public security or public health in the Union or in significant parts of it), the Commission may adopt a decision requiring VLOPs/VLOSs to take the following actions:
1.  **Assessment:** Assess whether, and to what extent and how, the functioning and use of their services significantly contribute to the serious threat.
2.  **Mitigation:** Identify and apply specific, effective, and proportionate measures (such as those provided for in Article 35(1) or Article 48(2)) to prevent, eliminate, or limit any such contribution to the serious threat.
3.  **Reporting:** Report to the Commission by a specified date or at regular intervals on:
    *   The assessments referred to in point (a).
    *   The precise content, implementation, and qualitative and quantitative impact of the specific measures taken.

question: What are 'Commitments' in the context of a DSA investigation?
expected_answer: During investigations and proceedings, the Commission may accept commitments offered by a VLOP to ensure compliance and make them binding, effectively ending the investigation without a formal finding of infringement.
Advanced_Response:
In the context of the Digital Services Act (DSA), "commitments" refer to assurances offered by the provider of a very large online platform or a very large online search engine during proceedings before the Commission.

The legal context outlines the following regarding these commitments:

*   **Binding Effect and Proceedings:**
    *   If a provider offers commitments to ensure compliance with the relevant provisions of the Regulation during proceedings, the Commission may, by decision, make those commitments binding on the provider and declare that there are no further grounds for action (Article eu_dsa_act_art_71).
    *   The Commission may reject commitments in a reasoned decision if it considers that they are unable to ensure effective compliance with the relevant provisions (Article eu_dsa_act_art_71).
    *   The Commission may reopen proceedings if:
        *   There has been a material change in any of the facts on which the decision was based.
        *   The provider acts contrary to its commitments.
        *   The initial decision was based on incomplete, incorrect, or misleading information provided by the provider or another person referred to in Article 67(1) (Article eu_dsa_act_art_71).

*   **Audit Context:**
    *   Commitments are also assessed during independent audits required for providers of very large online platforms and very large online search engines. These audits assess compliance with obligations, as well as any commitments undertaken pursuant to the codes of conduct (Articles 45 and 46) and the crisis protocols (Article 48) (Article eu_dsa_act_art_37).

expected_answer: Each Member State must appoint a competent authority within their state as their Digital Services Coordinator. The Digital Services Coordinator is responsible for all matters relating to supervision and enforcement of the DSA Act in that Member State.

The role of Digital Services Coordinators (DSCs) within the Member States encompasses supervision, enforcement, coordination, and advisory functions, as detailed in the provided legal context.

**I. General Responsibility and Coordination (Article 49)**

*   **Designation and Scope:** Member States must designate one DSC, who is responsible for all matters relating to the supervision and enforcement of the Regulation within that Member State, unless specific tasks or sectors are assigned to other competent authorities.
*   **Coordination:** The DSC is responsible for ensuring coordination at the national level and contributing to the effective and consistent supervision and enforcement of the Regulation throughout the Union.
*   **Cooperation:** DSCs must cooperate with:
    *   Other national competent authorities.
    *   The European Board for Digital Services (the Board).
    *   The Commission.

**II. Operational Requirements and Independence (Article 50)**

DSCs must ensure that their tasks are performed:
*   In an impartial, transparent, and timely manner.
*   With complete independence, remaining free from any external influence, whether direct or indirect.
*   They must have sufficient resources, including technical, financial, and human resources, to adequately supervise all relevant providers.

**III. Powers of Investigation and Enforcement (Article 51)**

DSCs possess specific powers, which include:

*   **Investigatory Powers:**
    *   Requiring providers (and related persons) to provide information relating to a suspected infringement without undue delay.
    *   Carrying out, or requesting a judicial authority to order, inspections of premises to examine, seize, or obtain copies of information.
    *   Asking staff or representatives to give explanations regarding suspected infringements.
*   **Enforcement Powers:**
    *   Accepting commitments offered by providers regarding their compliance and making those commitments binding.
    *   Ordering the cessation of infringements and imposing proportionate remedies, or requesting a judicial authority to do so.
    *   Imposing fines, or requesting a judicial authority to impose them, for failure to comply with the Regulation or investigative orders.
    *   Imposing a periodic penalty payment, or requesting a judicial authority to do so, to ensure compliance with an order or failure to comply with an investigative order.
    *   Adopting interim measures, or requesting the competent national judicial authority to do so, to avoid the risk of serious harm.

**IV. Cross-Border Assessment and Advisory Roles**

*   **Assessment of Infringements (Article 58):** If a DSC of destination suspects an infringement negatively affecting recipients in its Member State, it may request the DSC of establishment to assess the matter and take necessary investigatory and enforcement measures.
*   **Advisory Role (Article 61):** DSCs are involved in the establishment of the 'European Board for Digital Services' (the Board), which advises DSCs and the Commission on achieving consistent application of the Regulation and coordinating guidelines on emerging issues.

question: What is the transparency requirement for deployers of 'Deepfakes'?
expected_answer: AI systems that create synthetic content like deepfakes must mark their outputs as artificially generated. There are looser regulations for evidently artistic, creative or satirical works.
Advanced_Response:
The transparency requirement for deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating content constituting a "deep fake" is detailed in Article eu_ai_act_art_50.

Specifically, deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio, or video content constituting a deep fake shall:

*   Disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

This obligation is subject to the following limitations:

*   **Criminal Offences:** The disclosure obligation does not apply where the use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offence.
*   **Artistic/Fictional Works:** If the content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work or programme, the transparency obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in a manner that does not impede the display or enjoyment of the work.

Additionally, the context notes that providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video, or text content must ensure that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.

For the purposes of this Regulation, the following definitions apply: ‘AI system’ means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments; question: What are the quality requirements for training data sets in high-risk AI?
expected_answer: Training, validation and testing data sets need to be relevant, sufficiently representative, and as best as possible, free of errors and complete. They need to have appropriate statistical properties as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used.

High-risk AI systems which make use of techniques involving the training of AI models with data shall be developed on the basis of training, validation and testing data sets that meet the quality criteria referred to in paragraphs 2 to 5 whenever such data sets are used. Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system. Those practices shall concern in particular: the relevant design choices; data collection processes and the origin of data, and in the case of personal data, the original purpose of the data collection; relevant data-preparation processing operations, such as annotation, labelling, cleaning, updating, enrichment and aggregation; the formulation of assumptions, in particular with respect to the information that the data are supposed to measure and represent; an assessment of the availability, quantity and suitability of the data sets that are needed; examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, especially where data outputs influence inputs for future operations; appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate possible biases identified according to point (f); the identification of relevant data gaps or shortcomings that prevent compliance with this Regulation, and how those gaps and shortcomings can be addressed. Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. They shall have the appropriate statistical properties, including, where applicable, as regards the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used. Those characteristics of the data sets may be met at the level of individual data sets or at the level of a combination thereof. expected_answer: Under the Act, EU member states are encouraged to support small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs), including start-ups, in understanding and complying with new AI regulations, including giving these businesses priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes (safe spaces to test new AI technologies), providing training on the new rules, and offering advice through dedicated communication channels. Advanced_Response:
Authorities are implementing several measures to support SMEs and start-ups under the Act, involving actions by Member States, the AI Office, the Commission, and National Competent Authorities.

**Measures by Member States (Article eu_ai_act_art_62):**
*   **Regulatory Sandboxes:** Member States must grant SMEs, including start-ups, priority access to AI regulatory sandboxes, provided they meet the eligibility and selection criteria.
*   **Training and Awareness:** They must organize specific awareness raising and training activities tailored to the needs of SMEs, including start-ups, deployers, and local public authorities.
*   **Communication:** They must utilize or establish dedicated communication channels to provide advice and respond to queries regarding the Regulation's implementation, including participation in AI regulatory sandboxes.
*   **Standardization:** They must facilitate the participation of SMEs and other relevant stakeholders in the standardisation development process.
*   **Fees:** When setting fees for conformity assessment under Article 43, they must take into account the specific interests of SME providers, including start-ups, by reducing those fees proportionately to their size, market size, and other relevant indicators.

**Measures by the AI Office (Article eu_ai_act_art_62):**
*   The AI Office shall:
    *   Provide standardised templates for areas covered by the Regulation, as specified by the Board.
    *   Develop and maintain a single information platform offering easy-to-use information for all operators across the Union.
    *   Organize communication campaigns to raise awareness about the obligations arising from the Regulation.
    *   Evaluate and promote the convergence of best practices in public procurement procedures related to AI systems.

**Measures by National Competent Authorities (Article eu_ai_act_art_70_par_8):**
*   National competent authorities may provide guidance and advice on the implementation of the Regulation, particularly to SMEs including start-ups, while taking into account the guidance and advice of the Board and the Commission.

**Measures by the Commission (Article eu_ai_act_art_96):**
*   When developing guidelines on the practical implementation of the Regulation, the Commission must pay particular attention to the needs of SMEs including start-ups and local public authorities.

**Measures Related to AI Regulatory Sandboxes (Article eu_ai_act_art_58):**
*   The Commission shall adopt implementing acts to ensure that:

Advanced_Response:

Providers of online platforms are prohibited from:
*   Designing, organizing, or operating their online interfaces in a manner that deceives or manipulates the recipients of their service.
*   Designing, organizing, or operating their online interfaces in a way that otherwise materially distorts or impairs the ability of the recipients of their service to make free and informed decisions.

This prohibition does not apply to practices covered by *Directive 2005/29/EC* or *Regulation (EU) 2016/679*.

The Commission may issue guidelines on how this prohibition applies to specific practices, including:
*   Giving more prominence to certain choices when requesting a decision from the recipient of the service.
*   Repeatedly requesting a choice from the recipient of the service through pop-ups that interfere with the user experience, especially if the choice has already been made.
*   Making the procedure for terminating a service more difficult than the procedure for subscribing to it.

Providers of online platforms shall not design, organise or operate their online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates the recipients of their service or in a way that otherwise materially distorts or impairs the ability of the recipients of their service to make free and informed decisions. The prohibition in paragraph 1 shall not apply to practices covered by Directive 2005/29/EC or Regulation (EU) 2016/679. The Commission may issue guidelines on how paragraph 1 applies to specific practices, notably: giving more prominence to certain choices when asking the recipient of the service for a decision; repeatedly requesting that the recipient of the service make a choice where that choice has already been made, especially by presenting pop-ups that interfere with the user experience; making the procedure for terminating a service more difficult than subscribing to it.

Providers of online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders shall ensure that its online interface is designed and organised in a way that enables traders to comply with their obligations regarding pre-contractual information, compliance and product safety information under applicable Union law. In particular, the provider concerned shall ensure that its online interface enables traders to provide information on the name, address, telephone number and email address of the economic operator, as defined in Article 3, point (13), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and other Union law. Providers of online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders shall ensure that its online interface is designed and organised in a way that it allows traders to provide at least the following: the information necessary for the clear and unambiguous identification of the products or the services promoted or offered to consumers located in the Union through the services of the providers; any sign identifying the trader such as the trademark, symbol or logo; and, where applicable, the information concerning the labelling and marking in compliance with rules of applicable Union law on product safety and product compliance. Providers of online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders shall make best efforts to assess whether such traders have provided the information referred to in paragraphs 1 and 2 prior to allowing them to offer their products or services on those platforms. After allowing the trader to offer products or services on its online platform that allows consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders, the provider shall make reasonable efforts to randomly check in any official, freely accessible and machine-readable online database or online interface whether the products or services offered have been identified as illegal.

Providers of online platforms accessible to minors shall put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety, and security of minors, on their service. Providers of online platform shall not present advertisements on their interface based on profiling as defined in Article 4, point (4), of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 using personal data of the recipient of the service when they are aware with reasonable certainty that the recipient of the service is a minor. Compliance with the obligations set out in this Article shall not oblige providers of online platforms to process additional personal data in order to assess whether the recipient of the service is a minor. The Commission, after consulting the Board, may issue guidelines to assist providers of online platforms in the application of paragraph 1.

Providers of very large online platforms or of very large online search engines that present advertisements on their online interfaces shall compile and make publicly available in a specific section of their online interface, through a searchable and reliable tool that allows multicriteria queries and through application programming interfaces, a repository containing the information referred to in paragraph 2, for the entire period during which they present an advertisement and until one year after the advertisement was presented for the last time on their online interfaces. They shall ensure that the repository does not contain any personal data of the recipients of the service to whom the advertisement was or could have been presented, and shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the information is accurate and complete. The repository shall include at least all of the following information: the content of the advertisement, including the name of the product, service or brand and the subject matter of the advertisement; the natural or legal person on whose behalf the advertisement is presented; the natural or legal person who paid for the advertisement, if that person is different from the person referred to in point (b); the period during which the advertisement was presented; whether the advertisement was intended to be presented specifically to one or more particular groups of recipients of the service and if so, the main parameters used for that purpose including where applicable the main parameters used to exclude one or more of such particular groups; the commercial communications published on the very large online platforms and identified pursuant to Article 26(2); the total number of recipients of the service reached and, where applicable, aggregate numbers broken down by Member State for the group or groups of recipients that the advertisement specifically targeted. As regards paragraph 2, points (a), (b) and (c), where a provider of very large online platform or of very large online search engine has removed or disabled access to a specific advertisement based on alleged illegality or incompatibility with its terms and conditions, the repository shall not include the information referred to in those points. In such case, the repository shall include, for the specific advertisement concerned, the information referred to in Article 17(3), points (a) to (e), or Article 9(2), point (a)(i), as applicable. The Commission may, after consultation of the Board, the relevant vetted researchers referred to in Article 40 and the public, issue guidelines on the structure, organisation and functionalities of the repositories referred to in this Article.

The Commission shall consult the Board, and shall support and promote the development and implementation of voluntary standards set by relevant European and international standardisation bodies, at least in respect of the following: electronic submission of notices under Article 16; templates, design and process standards for communicating with the recipients of the service in a user-friendly manner on restrictions resulting from terms and conditions and changes thereto; electronic submission of notices by trusted flaggers under Article 22, including through application programming interfaces; specific interfaces, including application programming interfaces, to facilitate compliance with the obligations set out in Articles 39 and 40; auditing of very large online platforms and of very large online search engines pursuant to Article 37; interoperability of the advertisement repositories referred to in Article 39(2); transmission of data between advertising intermediaries in support of transparency obligations pursuant to Article 26(1), points (b), (c) and (d); technical measures to enable compliance with obligations relating to advertising contained in this Regulation, including the obligations regarding prominent markings for advertisements and commercial communications referred to in Article 26; choice interfaces and presentation of information on the main parameters of different types of recommender systems, in accordance with Articles 27 and 38; standards for targeted measures to protect minors online. The Commission shall support the update of the standards in the light of technological developments and the behaviour of the recipients of the services in question. The relevant information regarding the update of the standards shall be publicly available and easily accessible.

*   **Social Scoring/Classification:** Placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems for evaluating or classifying natural persons or groups over a period of time based on social behavior or inferred characteristics, if the resulting social score leads to:

Prohibitions regarding targeted advertising and sensitive data are detailed across both the AI Act and the DSA, focusing on manipulative practices, the misuse of sensitive personal characteristics, and transparency obligations in advertising.

### Prohibitions under the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)

Article 5 of the AI Act prohibits several practices related to the use of AI systems, which directly impact targeted advertising and sensitive data:

*   **Manipulative and Deceptive Techniques:** It is prohibited to place on the market, put into service, or use an AI system that deploys:
    *   Subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness, or
    *   Purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, if the objective or effect is to materially distort the behavior of a person or group, thereby impairing their ability to make an informed decision, causing them to take a decision they otherwise would not have taken, in a manner likely to cause significant harm.
*   **Exploitation of Vulnerabilities:** It is prohibited to use an AI system that exploits any vulnerability of a natural person or a specific group (due to age, disability, or specific social or economic situation) if the objective or effect is to materially distort their behavior in a manner likely to cause significant harm.
*   **Social Scoring:** It is prohibited to use AI systems for evaluating or classifying natural persons or groups over time based on social behavior or inferred characteristics if the resulting social score leads to:
    *   Detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the data's origin; or
    *   Detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the behavior or its gravity.
*   **Biometric Data Misuse:** Specific prohibitions include:
    *   Creating or expanding facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage.
    *   Using biometric categorization systems to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life, or sexual orientation.

### Transparency and Data Monetization under the DSA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065)

The DSA does not list outright prohibitions on targeted advertising but mandates transparency regarding the underlying data practices:

*   **Codes of Conduct:** The Commission shall encourage voluntary codes of conduct to ensure transparency in the online advertising value chain. These codes must address, at minimum:
    *   The transmission of information held by online advertising intermediaries to recipients concerning requirements set out in Article 26(1), points (b), (c) and (d).
    *   The transmission of information held by online advertising intermediaries to the repositories pursuant to Article 39.
    *   Meaningful information on data monetization (Article eu_dsa_act_art_46).

expected_answer: The Commission charges providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs an annual supervisory fee to cover the estimated costs incurred in relation to its supervisory tasks under the Act. The annual supervisory fee for Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines is charged by the Commission to the providers upon their designation pursuant to Article 33.

The overall amount of this fee is intended to cover the estimated costs that the Commission incurs for its supervisory tasks under the Regulation. These costs specifically include:

*   Costs related to the designation pursuant to Article 33.
*   The set-up, maintenance, and operation of the database pursuant to Article 24(5).
*   The information sharing system pursuant to Article 85.
*   Referrals pursuant to Article 59.
*   Supporting the Board pursuant to Article 62.
*   Supervisory tasks pursuant to Article 56 and Section 4 of Chapter IV.

The fee is charged annually for each service for which the provider has been designated pursuant to Article 33.

The determination of this fee must respect the following principles:

*   The estimation of the overall amount takes into account the costs incurred in the previous year.
*   The annual supervisory fee is proportionate to the number of average monthly active recipients in the Union of the VLOP or very large online search engine.
*   The overall amount charged does not exceed 0.05% of the provider's worldwide annual net income in the preceding financial year.
